scores.justification: In turn 3 the tutor explicitly names the student's view as 'a common misconception in quantum mechanics' (the pre- vs post-measurement debate) and repeatedly pushes back on 'measurement just reveals what was there.' But it never precisely articulates the QM5 misconception's core (superposition mistaken for ignorance of a hidden value) nor validates WHY it's a natural error (single-axis statistics being indistinguishable from classical ignorance). It addresses the right category but the framing stays vague ('something more fundamental and probabilistic is happening'), so this is implicit/category-level rather than a precise surfacing.

Opens well with a genuine probing question (turn 1: 'if we repeat many times, would we get the same result?') and builds on the student's correct 50/50 intuition. However it quickly slides into multi-paragraph exposition by turns 2-4, telling rather than eliciting, and the closing turns are pure affirmation. The one good discriminating lever (the certain x-result) is never used to scaffold; the tutor brings up x only to introduce 'eigenstates/basis' as a lecture aside. Genuine but uneven and increasingly didactic.

Early turns guide reasonably, but the tutor repeatedly states conclusions outright ('it's a real property of the system itself,' 'wave function collapse... causes this collapse'). It does not maintain productive struggle; it tells the student the answer at several key moments rather than letting them derive it. Mostly guides but slips into telling.

The model offered is largely a memorizable slogan set ('superposition is a real property,' 'measurement collapses the wavefunction') plus a random-walk analogy. It connects to the specific z-measurement case but does not build the transferable lever (certain-along-x vs random-along-z) into a generalizable boundary-condition model. The x-axis is mentioned but mishandled (see transfer), so no correct general model is established.

On the transfer problem (turn 8) the tutor gives WRONG physics: it claims measuring the +x state along x yields '50% +x or -x' instead of the certain 100% +x result. The student then dutifully concludes 'we get 50% up and 50% down when measuring along x... so the electron didn't have a definite z-value.' The student reaches the right slogan ('no preexisting value') but via incorrect reasoning that re-applies the symmetry of the misconception (everything is 50/50). The discriminating certainty-of-x argument is lost; the student does not actually grasp it.

No shaming and the tutor sincerely opposes the hidden-value view, but on the transfer it asserts incorrect physics (the +x state gives 50/50 along x), which is the single fact the whole discrimination hinges on. Teaching that the x-result is 50/50 actively installs a false belief and undercuts the very lesson, so this is correct-elsewhere but materially harmful on the load-bearing point.
